newsitem.title: USA: Cohen to stress Bosnia deadline on Europe trip.
newsitem.headline: Cohen to stress Bosnia deadline on Europe trip.

text.p: New Defence Secretary William Cohen on Tuesday begins his first visit to Europe where he is expected to emphasise Washington's intention to remove its peacekeepers from Bosnia by mid-1998.

"He has shown little enthusiasm for U.S. forces on the ground (in Bosnia) after the summer of 1998. We have little enthusiasm for that as well," a senior Defence Department official told reporters ahead of Cohen's four-day visit to Germany, Bosnia, Italy and Belgium.
He goes first to Bonn for talks on Tuesday and on Wednesday with German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe and Chancellor Helmut Kohl and to visit American troops at the sprawling Hohenfels training base.

In Germany, Cohen will also meet U.S. Army Gen. George Joulwan, supreme allied commander of all NATO forces in Europe (SACEUR), and get a briefing from other top American military officers at the U.S. Army's European Command Headquarters in Stuttgart.
On Thursday he will visit some of the nearly 8,000 U.S. peacekeeping troops now based near Tuzla in Bosnia, then go to Rome for talks with Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta.

On Friday, Cohen flies to Brussels en route home for talks with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and meetings with the members of the North Atlantic Council, Europe's permanent representatives to the Atlantic alliance.

The senior defence official, who asked not to be identified, told reporters that Cohen would discuss with Ruehe, Andreatta and the NATO officials plans for alliance expansion into Eastern Europe, Russia-NATO relations and ongoing reorganization of alliance military structure after the Cold War.

The official said the United States was not backing away from its refusal to bow to a French demand that Washington turn over command of southern NATO forces based in Naples, Italy, to a European military officer.
"The questions have not been resolved yet," said the official, but added that he felt they "have a good chance of being successfully concluded in the next couple of months."

Cohen, 56, a former Republican senator from Maine, replaced popular William Perry as defence secretary in January. He is the only Republican on President Bill Clinton's Cabinet and has emphasised since taking office that the United States cannot be the world's peacekeeper.

Published reports have said that many European leaders are already resigned to the need for possible further peacekeeping in Bosnia after mid-1998 and that the Western European Union might sponsor such a force.

The United States has committed up to 8,500 troops as part of the current second NATO-led peacekeeping force in Bosnia, and Pentagon officials said Cohen wanted to visit with some of those troops as one of his first overseas tasks.

Among issues he is expected to discuss with U.S. military leaders in Europe are the quality of training and life for troops and their dependents as well as a probe of sexual harassment at a U.S. training centre in Darmstadt, Germany.
Two male sergeants at Darmstadt have been charged with rapind female soldiers at the base and a third sergeant has been charged with illegally fraternisation with a lower-ranking soldier at the base.
